headline: The Race at 3.8 Knots: Neap Tide Softens the Rips, Sea Bass Fill the Gap
subhead: A first-quarter neap has taken the bite out of the strongest water on the coast, but Plum Gut structure and dawn bass are still paying off for those who adjust the clock.
body_markdown:
3.8 knots max ebb through the Race yesterday afternoon — soft by our standards. On a big spring tide this time of year I'm seeing 5, sometimes 5.5 knots ripping past Valiant Rock, current so hard it'll strip drag off a reel just holding bottom. This week's first-quarter neap has taken the teeth out of it, and that changes everything about how you fish this water.

Here's the practical version: slack at Valiant Rock has been running about 20 minutes longer than it does on a full moon spring tide, which means the window to get wire line down and bucktails ticking bottom without getting swept into the boulder field is wider than usual — good for guys who don't want to fight the current to get a bait in the zone, bad for anyone counting on the rip to concentrate bait and fish the way it does when the water's really moving. New London buoy readings are holding at 69.4°F, and that's mild enough that stripers in this stretch of the Sound have settled into the same low-light pattern we're seeing coastwide — they want dawn, dusk, or full dark, and they want it around structure where bait gets pinned.

Bass fishing has been a night-and-dawn game at Race Rock and along the Valiant Rock ledge, 40 to 60 feet, wire line with bunker spoons or a big Danny-style swimmer worked slow, or bucktails with a chunk of pork rind bounced right on the rock pile at the top of the tide change. Daytime has been mostly quiet unless you're marking a bait ball on the meter and can get a bucktail down into it fast — I had one solid fish, mid-30s, come off a jig dropped through a bunker school stacked over the eastern edge of Race Rock on the last of an incoming tide, but that was one fish in three hours of otherwise dead water. That's the honest read right now: the bass are here, they're just not eating on your schedule during daylight.

Sea bass have been the more dependable story. Structure around Plum Gut and out toward the Sluiceway is holding good numbers, and there's a 28-inch, right around 5-pound fish that came off the Gut structure recently that tells you the quality is there if you're willing to work bottom rigs with squid strips or Gulp on 3/4-ounce jigheads in 40 to 55 feet. The current through the Gut has been manageable enough on this neap to actually hold bottom without a ton of extra weight, which is a nice change from the spring tide slugfest where you're dragging 8 ounces just to stay down.

Fluke remain the most consistent thing going in this entire zone. Drifting the edges of the Sluiceway and the flats off Great Gull Island with white or chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on bucktails, 25 to 35 feet, moving water — outgoing has been better than incoming this week — keeps putting keepers in the box. It's not a blitz, but it's steady, and steady is worth something when everything else is working on a delay.

Albies and bonito haven't shown yet in the Gut or around Little Gull Island, but the water's getting into the range where I start paying attention — Montauk's reading 69.1°F and that end of the Island typically sees the first scouting fish before we do out here. I've got epoxy jigs rigged and ready on two rods, because when they show up around the Gut it's usually with almost no notice — one morning there's nothing, the next there's a rip full of nervous water and green backs slashing bait on the surface. If I had to guess, we're two to three weeks out, but that's a guess built on temperature trend, not a promise.

We flagged the offshore piece last week — said warm filament water pushing toward the CT grounds would put tuna within range of boats running south out of Sound ports, and that's exactly what's playing out. It's a longer run than most of what I cover in the Race and the Gut, but a few boats out of New London and Groton have made the run and found fish, which tells you the same warm water pattern that's kept our bass nocturnal is also stacking bait and predators further offshore.

Looking ahead: this neap holds through the weekend, and I'd use the wider slack windows at Valiant Rock and Race Rock to fish structure you normally can't hold bottom on — deeper boulder fields, the base of the Gut's eastern edge — with bucktails and wire line during the dawn push. Once we roll back toward a stronger tide midweek, expect the rips to tighten up again and the bass bite to concentrate hard into those short slack windows, which is when this water does what it's famous for. Keep the epoxy jigs rigged. Watch Little Gull Island for the first nervous water. That's usually how it starts out here.
